clue.text: Northerner who is ruddy rosy?

parts.note: a person from a county in north-west England whose emblem in the Wars of the Roses was a red rose, so 'ruddy rosy' describes his flower

explanation.surface: A question about some red-faced person from the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' suggests a flushed complexion, but it points to the red rose of the House of Lancaster; Lancashire is a county in north-west England whose people carry that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Lancashire, a northern English county whose symbol is the red rose, fits a red-rose northerner.

clue.text: A girl getting educated has no time for song

indicators.note: the clue says the letter for time, T, is missing from the girl's name

parts.note: Educating Rita is Willy Russell's play and film about a hairdresser studying literature, so the girl being educated is Rita

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl so busy with her studies that she has no time to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: Educating Rita is a well-known British play and film by Willy Russell, about a hairdresser who goes back to study; 'has no time' takes T out of her name.
explanation.definitionFit: An aria is a solo vocal piece in an opera, so it is a kind of song.

clue.text: Plant person winning the cup, not second!

indicators.note: the second letter of the winner's title is to be left out

parts.note: whoever wins the trophy is the champion

explanation.surface: A cup winner who certainly did not come second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not second' looks like praise for the winner, but it removes the second letter, H, from CHAMPION.
explanation.definitionFit: Campion is a wild flower with pink or white blooms, a common hedgerow plant.

clue.text: Urgent appeal over nothing makes one indifferent

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, that is above, the next one

parts.note: SOS is the international distress signal, an urgent call for help
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone who cries for help over nothing ends up not caring.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so describes something middling or mediocre, neither good nor bad.

clue.text: Small mammal managed to consume two hundred ducks!

indicators.note: the first word swallows the later pieces, holding them inside it

parts.note: to have managed a business is to have run it
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two hundred is CC
a duck is a zero score in cricket, written O, so ducks gives OO

explanation.surface: An animal that has managed to eat two hundred ducks, an absurd feast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To consume' signals that the word for managed swallows the other pieces. In cricket a duck is a score of nought, written like the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: The raccoon is a ringtailed North American mammal of modest size.

clue.text: Little creatures at the back end of pachyderms

indicators.note: only the tail end of the word for pachyderms is kept, its front being dropped

parts.note: pachyderms are thick-skinned beasts such as elephants

explanation.surface: Tiny insects crawling around the rear of some elephants.
explanation.walkthrough: The pachyderms are ELEPHANTS; keeping only the back end drops ELEPH and leaves the last four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ants are tiny insects, so they are little creatures.

clue.text: Use a ruler as specified and refuse to do anything further?

definitions.meaning: literally, mark a straight stroke with a ruler
set a limit beyond which one will not go

explanation.definitionFit: Ruling a straight mark on paper is the literal act; the idiom means setting a firm limit on what one will accept.

clue.text: Felines as asset with mice around

indicators.note: the letters are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: Cats regard mice scurrying about as a valuable resource.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' signals an anagram of AS ASSET plus MICE, eleven letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: Siamese cats are a pale, blue-eyed breed of domestic feline.

clue.text: Unfriendly rugby player, one given order to keep quiet

parts.note: the stand-off is the rugby union half-back also called fly-half
I is the Roman numeral for one
sh is the command for silence

explanation.surface: A surly rugby player who has been told to keep his mouth shut.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the stand-off (fly-half) is the back who usually directs play from behind the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone standoffish is aloof and reserved, the opposite of warm.

clue.text: Ounce of drug writer brought up concealed in cooking fat

parts.note: snow is slang for cocaine

indicators.note: the reversed writer is hidden inside the word for cooking fat

parts.note: lard is rendered pig fat used in cooking

indicators.note: in a down clue the writer's name is read upwards, that is backwards

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American author

explanation.surface: An ounce of some drug that a writer hid in a pot of cooking fat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ounce' looks like a weight, but it is a big cat. 'Brought up' reverses the writer's name in this down clue, and 'concealed in' puts it inside the fat.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is an old name for the snow leopard, a big cat of Central Asian mountains.

clue.text: Stage entertainer disguised as Persian ogre

indicators.note: the letters appear in a disguise, rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: A performer in costume, made up to look like a Persian monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disguised as' signals an anagram of PERSIAN OGRE.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera singer performs on stage, so is a kind of stage entertainer.

clue.text: A hill to the west featured in list

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means reading from right to left, backwards

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A hill towards the west appears on some inventory.
explanation.walkthrough: A TOR is a rocky hilltop in south-west England; 'to the west' reverses A TOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is a roster of duties, which is a kind of list.

clue.text: Son gets sleep in break

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep

explanation.surface: A boy gets some sleep during a break.
explanation.definitionFit: To snap is to break suddenly, as a twig does.

clue.text: Bringer of victory, endlessly obdurate

parts.note: a win is a victory

indicators.note: the last letter of the word for obdurate is cut off

parts.note: stony means hard and unyielding

explanation.surface: A tribute to a stubborn war leader who brought triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes Churchill, the wartime prime minister known for his stubborn resolve; STONY loses its end Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Churchill, Britain's leader in the Second World War, led the nation to triumph and was famously stubborn.

clue.text: Possible reason why one can't have tennis group

definitions.text: Possible reason why one can't have tennis
definitions.meaning: a tennis court lacking the mesh barrier across its middle cannot be played on
a set of nine performers or nine things

explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a set of nine musicians; split in two, the word describes a court missing its central barrier.

clue.text: Job was cut short — Rex in late forties or fifties?

parts.note: a post is a job or position

indicators.note: the word was loses its final letter

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A job ended early, and the king was in his late forties or fifties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut short' drops the S from WAS. 'Forties or fifties' looks like a person's age but means the years after 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: Postwar means after the Second World War, which ended in 1945, so the late 1940s and the 1950s.

clue.text: River reaches old city joined by southern streams

parts.note: the Po is the longest river in Italy
Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A river flows past an ancient city and on to the south.
explanation.definitionFit: To pour is to flow in a steady stream, so pours means streams.

clue.text: Impracticable whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: the letters read the same forwards or backwards, so either direction gives the same result

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Something unworkable from every angle.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a palindrome: it reads the same from either end, which is what 'whichever way you look at it' means.
explanation.definitionFit: Not on is a British idiom for unacceptable or not feasible.

clue.text: Walk from house, meeting old female

explanation.surface: Someone strolls out of a house and meets an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoof it is slang for going on foot.

clue.text: Sediment in bottle, essentially

indicators.note: the answer lies in the run of letters across the words that follow

explanation.surface: The dregs at the bottom of a wine bottle are what matters most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points to letters hidden across 'bottle, essentially'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lees are the dregs that settle at the bottom of wine.

clue.text: Beast with face of dark hair

parts.note: a bear is a large beast

indicators.note: the face, or front, of the word dark is its first letter

explanation.surface: An animal with a dark-haired face.
explanation.definitionFit: A beard is the hair growing on a man's chin and cheeks.

clue.text: Craftsman responsible for American stories

parts.note: the American spelling stories means the floors of a building, so this is the tradesman who raises buildings rather than a storyteller

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stories' looks like tales, but in American English it is the spelling of storeys, the floors of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who constructs houses puts up their floors, the storeys American English spells stories.

clue.text: Furnishing for top people with money shows good taste

parts.note: decor is the furnishing and decoration of a room
U stands for upper class, the top people

explanation.surface: Smart furniture for the wealthy elite shows refined taste.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the old British label for upper-class usage, so it stands for top people.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorum is propriety and correct behaviour, a sense of what is fitting.

clue.text: Bumpkin squashing newt gets ignored

indicators.note: the first word squeezes the second inside it

parts.note: a lout is a clumsy, uncouth person
an eft is a newt

explanation.surface: A country oaf squashes a newt and gets no attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squashing' puts the newt inside the bumpkin; an eft is an old word for a young newt.
explanation.definitionFit: To be left out is to be excluded or passed over.

clue.text: Attack sees nose put out of joint

indicators.note: something out of joint is dislocated, so the letters are displaced into a new order

explanation.surface: An assault leaves someone with a dislocated nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of joint' signals an anagram of NOSE PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To set upon someone is to assault them.

clue.text: Northern estate — a cosy place to live

parts.note: Est is an abbreviation for estate, as on maps and addresses; that the letters also run unbroken across the two clue words is a coincidence, with no hiding signal

explanation.surface: A northern housing estate is a snug spot to make a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest is a snug home, as a bird builds or as in 'love nest'.

clue.text: Dish contributing to starters

indicators.note: the answer is part of the following word, contributing letters to it

explanation.surface: A dish that forms part of the starters on a menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contributing to' means the answer is found inside 'starters'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tart is a pastry case with filling, a dish served sweet or savoury.

clue.text: Your writer, shut up in trap

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as your writer, giving me
sh means be quiet

explanation.surface: The setter says to be quiet while caught in a trap.
explanation.definitionFit: To mesh is to catch in a net, ensnare.

clue.text: Bank of Scotland gives support to leader of enterprise

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment

indicators.note: the leader of the word enterprise is its first letter

explanation.surface: A Scottish bank backs the head of a business venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank of Scotland' looks like the financial institution but means a Scottish hillside.
explanation.definitionFit: A brae is a Scots word for a hillside or slope.

clue.text: Monk — busy type over the course of day

indicators.note: the busy type spans the day, so D sits within it

parts.note: a bee is proverbially busy

explanation.surface: A monk is a busy worker throughout the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the course of' puts D inside BEE. The Venerable Bede was an English monk and historian.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venerable Bede was an English monk and historian of the eighth century.

clue.text: Like Hannah — or rohan!

definitions.meaning: Hannah of the 1924 song, the vamp of Savannah who was famously cold to her lovers
the middle letter of rohan is H, the pencil grade standing for firm lead, so it has H at its centre

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition plays on H, the pencil grade meaning hard, sitting at the heart of 'rohan'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's Hannah is unfeeling and cruel; rohan has H, the pencil code for firm, at its core.

clue.text: Old court's formality coming with cautionary signal

parts.note: starch means stiffness or formality of manner
amber is the traffic light warning drivers to take care

explanation.surface: An old court's stiffness goes with a warning light.
explanation.walkthrough: The Star Chamber was an English court abolished in 1641, known for arbitrary judgments.
explanation.definitionFit: The Star Chamber was a historic English court sitting at Westminster.
